etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From older kare → are. Compound of あ (a, “that, yon”) + れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The long form of あ (a, “I, me”). From あ (a) + れ (-re, nominalizing suffix)
Fell into disuse in roughly the Heian period, when it was replaced by われ (ware).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Multiple possible derivations.
* During the Edo period, restaurants specializing in large portions were called 慳貪屋 (kendon'ya), from 慳貪 (kendon, “greedy”, in reference to “very hungry”) + 屋 (ya, “house, store, restaurant”). The serving bowls were called 慳貪振り鉢 (kendon-buri-bachi), literally “greedy” + “in that fashion” + “bowl”. The ken portion was elided, producing donburi-bachi, and then the -hachi was dropped to produce donburi.
* Alternatively, and perhaps more likely, donburi in reference to “a bowl filled with large amount of food” may be cognate with どんぶり (donburi), an onomatopoeia of something heavy plunking into deep water, or something big and soft plopping down, related to onomatopoeia どぶり (doburi), どぶん (dobun), どんぶ (donbu), and どん (don), all of generally similar meanings. The food starts with a large portion of rice, also referred to as 丼飯 (donburi meshi), which could be analyzed as “plopped-down rice”.
: Donburi is also used to refer to something “rough, approximate, not finely worked”, as in the phrase 丼勘定 (donburi kanjō, “rough approximation, loose estimate”). This is consistent with a derivation from the onomatopoeia, but not from the restaurant terms.
The kanji spelling shows 井 (“a well”) with a dot in the center, possibly indicating something thrown into the well. This could suggest that the Middle Chinese reading tom^X may similarly derive from onomatopoeia.

etymologies.heading: Etymology

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Classical Japanese 咥(くは)ふ (kufafu). Possibly related to 食(く)う (kuu, “to eat; to grab with one's mouth”, historical form 食(く)ふ (kufu)), with auxilliary verb ふ (-fu), expressing repetition or ongoing state.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Spelling repurposed from nyoshō below during the Meiji period (1868–1912), using the relatively newer kan'on readings of the characters.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Middle Chinese 女性 (MC nrjoX sjengH, “woman; female + character; gender”). The goon, so likely the initial borrowing.
Largely superseded in everyday Japanese by josei above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 対(たい) (tai, “place in opposition and compare”) + 照(しょう) (shō, “check one thing against another”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Rearrangement of 和平 (wahei, “peace”), likely that 平 (hei) also means "flat", therefore switching the kanji meant "calm, equal + harmony → peace".
First attested in the Meiji era.

etymologies.text: Derived from the verb 正す (tadasu, “to correct”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from the nominal form 正し (tadashi, “correcting”) of the verb 正す (tadasu, “to correct”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in the early 800s.
Speculatively, may be an ancient resultative noun derived from verb 増す (masu, “to increase; to excel, to be excellent; to stand out, to be outstanding”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from the classical terminal form masashi of modern adjective 正しい (masashii, “true, real, certain”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
深(ふか) (fuka, root of 深(ふか)い (fukai, “deep, profound”)) + める (-meru, “-ify, -en”), developed from Classical Japanese 深(ふか)む (fukamu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Pseudo-loan from Chinese, a reformation of 物(もの)騒(さわ)がしい (monosawagashii, na-adjective). Alternatively, from 物忩(ぶっそう) (bussō).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 画(が) (ga, “picture, drawing, painting”) + 家(か) (-ka, “expert, professional, performer”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: A 国字 (kokuji, “Japanese-coined character”). A ligature (合字) of 火(は)田(た) (hata), originally written vertically as ⿱火田.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Man’yōshū, completed sometime after 759 CE. In turn from reconstructed Proto-Japonic *patakay. Compare Korean 밭 (bat, “dry field”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, attested in the Izumo Fudoki completed in 733.
By surface analysis, 杵 (ki, “mallet, pounder, pestle”, from which きね (kine) “pestle” is also derived) + 築く (tsuku, “to build up, to pile up, to amass”, see below), for a base sense of “to make something using a pounder or mallet”, much as when building up rammed earth or stonework.
This term as 杵 (ki, “pounder”) + 築く (tsuku, “build up”) then underwent conflation with, or was reanalysed as, 城 (ki, “castle, fortress”) + 築く (tsuku, “build up”) with a basic sense of “to construct”. This latter derivation is given as the only etymology in some references. However, the “to construct” sense is attested centuries later in 1081. Moreover, the “castle, fortress” sense for the initial ki- element was pronounced in Old Japanese as /ki₂/, while the “pounder, mallet” sense was pronounced /ki₁/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Thought to be from 見(み) (mi, “seeing, looking”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)る (miru, “to see, to look”)) + 留(と)める (tomeru, “to hold, to keep, to remain”), possibly with semantics like “to keep one's vision on” → “to recognize, to acknowledge, to observe”.
